Otto von Bismarck examines US backchannel 'diplomacy' in Moscow:

Rain tapped against the tall windows of the Friedrichsruh estate. Prince Otto von Bismarck sat behind a massive oak desk covered with maps of Eastern Europe and printed intelligence dispatches dated early September 2026. Across from him, Dr Helen Vance, a senior strategic analyst, adjusted a stack of cables detailing diplomatic movements between Washington, Moscow, and Kyiv.

Bismarck picked up a summary sheet, holding it close to his eyes. He pointed a thick finger at three names printed near the top: Jared Kushner, Steve Witkoff, and John Ratcliffe.

"Explain this delegation to me again," Bismarck said, his voice deep and raspy. "Washington sends a real estate developer and a son in law to the Kremlin to negotiate the end of a major European war. Eleven days prior, the director of their central intelligence agency arrives in secret to 'deliver warnings'. Is this a coherent state strategy or an act of theatrical desperation?"

Helen leaned forward. "President Donald Trump favours personal representatives over career foreign service officers. Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are his trusted envoys. They arrived in Moscow on Saturday, 5 September 2026, meeting Vladimir Putin for three hours inside the Kremlin. They brought what Washington calls a 'concrete peace proposal'. They plan to travel directly to Kyiv next to present the same framework to Volodymyr Zelensky."

Bismarck leaned back in his heavy leather chair, resting his hands on his stomach. "Back channel diplomacy is the standard currency of serious statecraft. Public diplomacy is mostly noise for domestic assemblies. When I negotiated with Saint Petersburg in 1887, we kept the Reinsurance Treaty hidden from the public and from our own allies in Vienna. But a back channel is merely a pipe. What matters is the pressure inside it. What leverage does Washington actually push through this pipe?"

"Very little to nothing right now," Helen replied. "That is the core problem. The US is simultaneously involved in a damaging military conflict with Iran. That war consumes American attention, naval assets, and air defence munitions. Ukraine faces severe shortages of Patriot missile interceptors because Washington has prioritised its own operational needs in the Middle East. Russia knows this. Russian forces have intensified their long range drone and missile attacks across Ukraine, exploiting those exact defensive gaps."

Bismarck nodded slowly, his gaze drifting to a map of the Black Sea coast. "So Washington sends envoys because its position is weakening, not because its position is strong. That is the first fundamental error. A state that seeks an emergency exit because its attention is divided elsewhere does not negotiate from strength. It begs for terms."

"CIA Director John Ratcliffe tried to counter that perception during his visit to Moscow late last month," Helen noted. "He warned Russian intelligence officials that escalating the conflict would backfire and that Russia's long term position would deteriorate. But the Kremlin largely ignored the warning. Within days, Russian strikes against Ukrainian infrastructure actually increased."

"Of course they increased," Bismarck said, a faint smile touching his moustache. "A warning unsupported by visible military force or a clear willingness to endure friction is not a deterrent. It's merely advice. When you tell an adversary that his position will deteriorate in the future, but he sees you running low on ammunition today, he calculates that your patience will break long before his reserves do. Words don't alter the balance of power. Only physical constraints and credible threats alter it."

Helen drew a fresh document from her folder. "There was one tactical concession. Both sides agreed to a 72 hour pause on air strikes against Kyiv and Moscow to allow Witkoff and Kushner to travel safely. The Kremlin presented this as a gesture of goodwill."

"It's not a concession," Bismarck countered sharply. "It's cheap theatre. A three day pause on bombing capitals costs the Kremlin nothing. It gives Russian missile crews time to reload, reassess target sets, and conduct reconnaissance. More importantly, it grants the Russian President the appearance of a reasonable statesman while altering zero structural facts on the ground. It creates a psychological trap for the American envoys. They feel they have achieved a breakthrough before negotiations have even begun, when in reality they have merely purchased three days of quiet in one city."

He stood up, walking slowly toward the wall map. He traced the front line running through Eastern Ukraine with his knuckle.

"Tell me about the American President's core model of this conflict," Bismarck requested. "How does he explain the war to himself?"

"Trump believes the war is fundamentally driven by personal hatred between Zelensky and Putin," Helen said. "He described it publicly as a personality problem that prevents a deal. His approach is transactional. He believes that if two skilled business negotiators present a framework on territory and security, both leaders can be persuaded to sign a deal and end the fighting."

Bismarck turned around, his eyes sharp. "That's a profound misunderstanding of international relations. You can't reduce a structural clash of state interests to a commercial dispute over real estate. Personalities matter on the margins, but sovereign states don't sacrifice hundreds of thousands of men and strain their entire societies because two leaders dislike each other. Russia is fighting to prevent Ukraine from becoming an integrated platform for Western military power. Ukraine is fighting for its national survival and territorial integrity. Those are existential objectives. They can't be resolved by splitting the difference on a map as if you were buying an office tower in Manhattan."

"What would a real peace mechanism require then?" Helen asked. "From a balance of power perspective?"

"A durable peace requires one of two conditions," Bismarck explained, pacing slowly across the rug. "Either one side suffers a total military defeat that destroys its capacity to resist, or both sides reach a point of absolute structural exhaustion where continuing the war is demonstrably more dangerous to their regime survival than stopping it. Neither condition exists today. Russia believes time is on its side because American focus is split by the war with Iran. Ukraine can't accept a frozen line that leaves it vulnerable to future destruction. Therefore, any paper agreement signed today without a permanent balance of enforcement behind it is merely an armistice. It's an operational pause before the next offensive."

"Is there no value in private envoys like Witkoff and Kushner?" Helen asked. "They argue that their lack of diplomatic baggage allows them to speak frankly with Putin in ways formal diplomats can't."

"Frank speech is useless if it's disconnected from institutional power," Bismarck replied. "When I negotiated on behalf of Prussia, the Russian court knew that my promises were backed by the Prussian army, the Ministry of Finance, and a permanent bureaucracy. Private envoys represent the personal preferences of an individual leader. What happens when the American presidency changes hands, or when domestic political pressure shifts in Washington? Putin knows that a personal deal with an envoy binds only the current administration. It does not bind the American state. A treaty that lacks institutional permanence offers no real security."

Helen looked down at the reports. "So when Witkoff and Kushner travel from Moscow to Kyiv, what are they actually accomplishing?"

"They're conducting an exercise in political management," Bismarck said flatly. "They're testing whether an adversary can be persuaded to give up at the negotiating table what he's currently winning on the battlefield. The answer will be no. Putin will speak politely, offer warm wishes for the American President, and encourage further talks. He'll do this because continuing the dialogue keeps Washington hopeful, delays stronger American military intervention, and exploits the division in Western strategy. But he'll not alter his strategic goals."

"And Ukraine?" Helen asked.

"Ukraine is trapped," Bismarck said quietly. "Kyiv must participate in the process to avoid alienating its primary benefactor in Washington. But Zelensky knows that accepting a deal without explicit, binding security guarantees is national suicide. So both sides will play their assigned roles in this diplomatic drama. They will observe the temporary pause, issue polite statements about substantive discussions, and then return to the battlefield the moment the envoys board their aircraft back to America."

Helen gathered her papers. "Then Washington is confusing the act of negotiation with the existence of leverage."

"Precisely," Bismarck said, sitting back down at his desk. "Diplomacy isn't a substitute for power. It's the algebra of power. It translates relative military strength, economic endurance, and strategic willpower into formal agreements. When you attempt to do diplomacy without underlying power, you're not engaging in statecraft. You're merely performing for an audience while your adversary advances."

He picked up a pen and drew a firm circle around the Black Sea on his map. "If Washington wishes to end this war, it must first resolve its own strategic overextension. It can't dictate terms in Eastern Europe while fighting in the Middle East with depleted arsenals. Until American power is reordered and concentrated, sending envoys to Moscow is not a path to peace. It is an admission of fatigue."

(Trump sent Ratcliffe, Kushner and Witkoff to Moscow in a desperate attempt to end America's losing war against Russia in Ukraine).

---

Otto von Bismarck (1815-1898) was a Prussian and German statesman who unified Germany in 1871 and served as its first chancellor. He shaped 19th century European diplomacy through realpolitik and established early social welfare programmes.

text:
Two minutes. That is how long an Arkansas jury took in November 1919 to sentence a sharecropper named William Wordlaw to die in the electric chair, and what he had done was join a union that asked landlords for a written statement of what their own cotton had earned. Wordlaw had made sixteen bales that year at two hundred and twenty-five dollars a bale, three thousand six hundred dollars in all, and he never saw a dollar of it, and the only reason anybody has that figure is that Ida B. Wells-Barnett talked her way into the penitentiary and asked him. He got out in 1923 and the record loses him completely after that, so if you want to know how this one ended, there is nobody who can tell you.

What Phillips County said about that union went out to the Helena World on the seventh of October, 1919, and it was built to be repeated.

It said the trouble in Phillips County was not a race riot. It said it was a deliberately planned insurrection, directed by an organization called the Progressive Farmers and Household Union of America, and that the union existed to band Black people together for the killing of white people.

The man who said it was E. M. Allen, a planter and real estate developer who had come down from the North in 1906 to make money and had made it. He was not a sheriff, a judge, or a coroner.

He was the spokesman, and by the time he spoke, the killing had been over for four days.

That sentence is the reason most Americans have never heard of Elaine. It held for the better part of eighty years, and it is still the shape of the story in some rooms in that county.

What the union had actually been asking for was a statement of account. Itemized, on paper.

That is the whole thing. That is what the men at Hoop Spur were organizing to get, and it is the thing nobody in Phillips County would put in their hands.

Sharecroppers in the Arkansas Delta were settled with once a year, after the crop came in. The planter weighed the cotton, the planter sold the cotton, the planter kept the books, and the planter announced at the end of it what was left over for the family that had grown it.

The family bought its seed, its meal, its shoes and its medicine at the plantation store on credit against that settlement, at prices the store set. Nobody audited any of it.

A sharecropper who asked to see the arithmetic was told the number and sent home. A sharecropper who kept asking could be run off the place, and there was an unwritten rule across the Delta that a Black tenant did not leave while a debt was on the books.

Cotton had gone from about eleven cents a pound in 1915 to about forty cents in 1919. For the first time in living memory there was real money in the fields, and the men working those fields could not find out how much of it was theirs.

In the fall of 1918, at his office in Little Rock, a white attorney named Ulysses S. Bratton began hearing from them. A man called Carter had worked ninety acres and watched his landlord take the entire crop and his possessions with it.

A farmer from Ratio told Bratton that the plantation manager there would not give the sharecroppers an itemized account for their cotton. Another described a landlord holding out to starve people into selling at his price.

Bratton took the work. He was hired to sue for the men's share of the 1919 crop, and what that meant in practice was forcing planters to produce, in court, the pages they had refused to produce in the settlement room.

The union that hired him had been put together by Robert L. Hill, a Black tenant farmer from Winchester with no organizing experience and a great deal of nerve. He told men to go out and each bring twenty-five more, and by that autumn there were seven lodges in Phillips County.

The Hoop Spur lodge kept officers the way any lodge does. Jim Miller was its president.

Ed Ware was its secretary, which is to say Ed Ware was the man who kept the union's written records in a county where written records were the whole argument.

Ed Ware had already refused to sell his own cotton for less than he thought it was worth. He had been threatened for it, up to and including talk of a rope.

By the last week of September he was thinking about quitting.

On the night of Tuesday, the thirtieth of September, about a hundred people came to a small Baptist church at Hoop Spur, three miles north of the town of Elaine. It was the lodge's third meeting.

They lit three lamps inside. The wooden benches filled fast.

Sallie Giles arrived around eight with her sons Albert and Milligan. Paul Hall was there, and Joe Knox, who people called Preacher, and Frank Moore with his wife.

Jim Miller and his wife Cleola came last, in a horse and buggy. Ed Ware never came at all.

Outside in the dark, armed men from the lodge stood watch along the road, because meetings like this one had been broken up before and listened in on before. One of them, waiting, said out loud that the whites were going to kill them.

Inside, the meeting opened with a prayer, the way all their meetings opened.

Around eleven o'clock a car stopped in front of the church. Three men were in it: W. A. Adkins, a white security officer for the Missouri Pacific Railroad, Charles Pratt, a white Phillips County deputy sheriff, and a Black trusty named Kid Collins.

There was a firefight in front of the church. Who fired first has never been settled and the accounts flatly contradict each other.

Adkins was killed. Pratt was wounded.

Collins was untouched, and he walked to a store and got on a telephone to Helena.

By morning the county was moving. The sheriff sent a posse, and the Helena American Legion post sent volunteers, some of them veterans lately home from France.

Word went out along both sides of the Mississippi River that Black people in Phillips County were fighting back. Between six hundred and a thousand armed white men came in from outside the county to hunt them.

They went through the Hoop Spur settlements, went into the houses of union members and carried out what was in them. Families ran into the canebrakes and the woods and stayed there.

The Arkansas Gazette reported the next day that at least fifteen bodies were lying in the streets and outskirts of Elaine, with more expected in the woods. A Memphis Press reporter watched men fire into corpses already lying on the road as they rode out of Helena.

The men on those roads were not being sorted by whether they had joined anything. Four brothers named Johnston were coming back from a squirrel hunt and had nothing to do with the union.

Two of them were doctors, one ran a car dealership in Helena, and the youngest, Leroy, had come home the year before from France and the regiment the world now calls the Harlem Hellfighters.

A white man they took for a friend warned them off the road and told them to catch the train instead. A posse stopped that train at Elaine, put them in handcuffs and into the back of a car, and they were killed and left on the roadside, on the first or the second of October depending on which account you read.

Leroy Johnston's Army service record turned out to have been deliberately altered. His family did not receive his Purple Heart until 2018.

On the morning of the second of October, 1919, the troop train came in from Camp Pike with more than five hundred soldiers and twelve machine guns, and Governor Charles Hillman Brough rode down with them. Colonel Isaac Jenks disarmed the town.

The mobs went home. The soldiers put several hundred Black people into stockades, where they were held until a white employer came to vouch for them by name.

Some were tortured there. Then they were moved to the jail in Helena, and the torture continued in the jail.

Two hundred and eighty-five people went into a building with room for forty-eight.

Two white men who did it later swore to it. H. F. Smiddy and T. K. Jones, both of whom had testified for the prosecution, gave sworn affidavits in 1921 admitting they had tortured prisoners in that jail to produce testimony, and naming other men who had done the same.

Ida B. Wells-Barnett got the rest of it directly from the men themselves. They told her they had been beaten and left for dead, given electric shocks, and drugged, all of it aimed at making them confess to a plot to kill white people.

Seven men in Helena appointed themselves to explain all of it while the jail was still full. The Committee of Seven was made up of officials, planters, and businessmen, and it had no legal authority whatsoever.

Governor Brough met them, gave them his blessing, and went back to Little Rock the next day. What he took away in exchange was their promise that there would be no lynchings in Phillips County.

He then told a press conference that the situation had been well handled, that there was no danger of lynching, and that the white citizens of the county deserved praise. Four days later the committee announced its finding, which was the insurrection, and E. M. Allen took it to the newspaper.

That promise cost the county nothing. It had agreed not to hang men from trees, and in return it was left alone to do the same work indoors, on paper, with a judge present.

On the twenty-seventh of October the grand jury met. By the thirty-first it had charged a hundred and twenty-two Black people with crimes ranging from nightriding to murder.

The trials opened on the third of November in front of Circuit Judge J. M. Jackson, with troops outside the courthouse to guarantee that nobody was lynched. Jackson appointed local white attorneys to defend the men.

Jacob Fink, appointed to represent Frank Hicks, told the jury outright that he had not interviewed a single witness. He asked for no change of venue and challenged no juror, taking the first twelve men called.

Frank Hicks was convicted of murder. The jury was out eight minutes.

That same day a fresh jury convicted Frank Moore, Ed Hicks, Joe Knox, Ed Coleman and Paul Hall of aiding and abetting the same killing, though there was no evidence that Coleman or Hall had anything to do with it. All of them got death.

The next day Alf Banks Jr. and John Martin, two of the men who had stood guard on the road outside the church, were convicted. The jury was out nine minutes.

William Wordlaw, another of the guards outside the church, was convicted the same day. The jury was out less than two minutes.

Wordlaw was twenty-two years old and farmed sixteen acres for a lumber company at Wabash. He told them he had been unarmed that night, and that after the shooting he had helped move women and children into the woods.

Wordlaw had made sixteen bales of cotton that season, worth two hundred and twenty-five dollars a bale, three thousand six hundred dollars in all, and he never saw the money. That is the only itemized statement in this entire story that anybody ever managed to write down.

It exists because Ida B. Wells-Barnett asked him, which is a thing nobody with any authority in Arkansas ever did. What became of William Wordlaw after he got out of prison is not known.

In that same first week of November, sixty-five other men took hurried pleas rather than face a jury of that kind, and drew sentences of up to twenty-one years.

Ed Ware, the secretary, was caught and tried last, on the seventeenth of November. The state's case against him rested on one man, Suggs Bondsman, who said he had overheard Ware and others naming planters to be killed.

That testimony was the only evidence of any plot introduced in any of these trials. Nobody cross-examined him.

When Scipio Africanus Jones finally did cross-examine him six months later, Bondsman could not name anyone else who had been at the meeting, and testified falsely that he had not been arrested.

Scipio Jones had been born enslaved and was the leading Black lawyer in Arkansas. During the retrials in Helena he slept at a different Black family's house every night because it was not safe to be found twice in the same bed.

The NAACP hired George Murphy, seventy-nine years old and a former Confederate officer, for three thousand dollars and expenses. Black families in Little Rock raised money for Scipio Jones themselves, in a state where their own settlements had never been itemized.

The men in the cells were not waiting quietly. On the thirtieth of December, 1919, one of the twelve sat down and wrote a letter to Ida B. Wells-Barnett in Chicago.

She took the train to Little Rock. She went to the address in the letter and talked with the wives first, then got herself into the penitentiary by claiming to be a visiting cousin, and spent the day with the men.

What she wrote afterward put the case in one line. Their crime, she said, was to organize for the market price of their cotton, to buy land, and "to employ a lawyer to get settlements of their accounts."

She also did the arithmetic nobody in Phillips County had done. Between the cotton and the corn taken off Black families during and after the killing, she reckoned the white men of that county had cleared about a million dollars in a year.

That million dollars had specific rooms in it. By Wells-Barnett's account, the furniture and clothes belonging to Frank Moore and his wife ended up with a white landowner named Bill Archdale and his family.

The papers that finally moved something were the Smiddy and T. K. Jones affidavits. Attached to a federal petition, two white men's sworn admissions of torture did what no Black man's testimony had been permitted to do.

In February 1923 the Supreme Court of the United States ruled in Moore v. Dempsey that a trial run under mob pressure, uncorrected by the state's own appeals courts, is not due process. It called the Helena proceeding a mask.

That decision changed American law. It did not open a single cell door.

The Court sent the case back down to the district court for a hearing, and that was all it did.

Six of the men, the Ware defendants, were freed in June 1923 by the Arkansas Supreme Court, on the ground that two terms of court had passed without the state bringing them to trial. The state simply never tried them again.

The other six, the Moore defendants, walked out in January 1925 on indefinite furloughs signed by Governor Thomas McRae in the last days of his term. The record disagrees on whether that was the thirteenth or the fourteenth.

They had pleaded guilty to second-degree murder to get there.

No furlough is a pardon. Not one of the twelve was ever cleared.

No white person was charged with anything.

The county's books closed like this. Five white men died, and those deaths were reported, investigated, and attached to names.

Four of them run all the way through the record: W. A. Adkins, Clinton Lee, James Tappan and O. R. Lilly.

Colonel Jenks also entered the death of one of his own soldiers in his report.

For the Black dead there is no such page. Jenks wrote that his troops killed two.

Military intelligence put the total at no more than twenty.

Walter White was told in Helena that more than a hundred had been killed. James Weldon Johnson estimated as many as four hundred.

A white Arkansas Gazette employee named Sharpe Dunaway published a book in 1925 claiming eight hundred and fifty-six, mostly killed by the soldiers, and offered almost no documentation for the number. Historians who have spent careers in the records generally land somewhere between one and two hundred, and say plainly that the figure is unknown.

The figure is unknown because nobody counted. There was no coroner's roll for them, no inquest, no list, no attempt.

The number you will see most often, two hundred and thirty-seven, comes from a 2015 investigation by the Equal Justice Initiative and now appears almost everywhere. It is an estimate and not a body count, and nobody has ever produced a list of two hundred and thirty-seven names.

Historians have recovered the names of only a small fraction of the people killed in Phillips County that week.

That is why the memorial dedicated in Helena in September 2019 is a cenotaph with no names on it. It carries one line, for those known and unknown, because there is no roll to carve.

More than a century later, the itemized statement is still owed. Not by the planters, who are gone, but by the record itself, which has never been made to show its work.

The record can still be added to. Census sheets, church rolls, deeds, pension files, family Bibles and the memories of the oldest person in your family are exactly the materials the professors and their students are using right now to pull names back out of that week, one at a time.

The men at Hoop Spur wanted their labor written down and totaled honestly. Phillips County called that an uprising and answered it with a killing nobody has ever counted, and the request has still not been granted.

Find one name. Write it down somewhere it can be read.

That is the settlement.
